✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

NOT A WOKE TRAP. Hamnet's feminist revisionism is front and center from the marketing, the source novel's reputation, and Zhao's own public statements about the project. O'Farrell's novel was celebrated in feminist literary circles before the film was ever greenlit. The film's marketing foregrounds Jessie Buckley as Agnes, not Paul Mescal as Shakespeare. There is no bait-and-switch here. Audiences know they are getting a story about Shakespeare's wife, not Shakespeare himself. The feminist elements are the advertised premise, not contraband smuggled inside traditional packaging. Some conservative viewers may object to the Agnes-as-wild-healer archetype or to Shakespeare being portrayed as emotionally absent, but these are visible from the trailer. There is no deception.

Hamnet (2025) - Full VirtueVigil Review

SPOILER ALERT - This review discusses the film's plot in full detail, including its ending. If you have not seen Hamnet and want to remain unspoiled, be warned: we do not hold back. Our readers deserve the complete picture before they watch.

1. Opening Hook - The Most Beautiful Film of 2025, and the Most Complicated

Chloe Zhao's Hamnet is a film that will make you cry. It will make the person next to you cry. It will make the hardened film critic three rows back cry. The question VirtueVigil has to answer is not whether it is beautiful or moving or exceptionally well-crafted. It is all of those things. The question is whether it is honest.

Based on Maggie O'Farrell's 2020 Women's Prize-winning novel, Hamnet dramatizes the life of William Shakespeare's family, centering on his wife Agnes (the name used in her father's will, used here to distinguish her from the actress Anne Hathaway) and the devastating death of their 11-year-old son Hamnet from the bubonic plague. The film's argument is that Hamlet, perhaps the greatest play ever written, was born from this private catastrophe, and that Agnes, not William, was the emotional engine of the household that made Shakespeare's art possible.

This is a feminist thesis. Let us be plain about that. But it is a feminist thesis that arrives inside one of the most genuinely traditional films Hollywood has produced in years: a story about marriage, parenthood, sacrifice, the death of a child, and art as a vessel for grief. There is no identity politics lecture. No race-swapping. No anachronistic modern ideology crowbarred into a period setting. There is only a family, a plague, and a father who turned his son's name into the most famous play in the English language.

That tension between its feminist perspective and its traditional content is what makes Hamnet such a fascinating case for VirtueVigil.

2. Plot Summary - Love, Plague, and the Birth of Hamlet

The film opens in the forests near Stratford-upon-Avon, where Agnes is depicted as a wild, intuitive woman who summons hawks, gathers herbs, and reads palms. She is the daughter of a woman rumored to be a forest witch. William Shakespeare is a young tutor struggling under the weight of his father's debts and expectations.

They meet. He tells her the story of Orpheus and Eurydice. She reads his palm and foresees his future: success, but also two children at her deathbed. They consummate their relationship in the forest. Agnes becomes pregnant. Her family disowns her. She moves in with the Shakespeares. They marry quickly.

Agnes gives birth to their first daughter Susanna in the woods. Later, confined by the Shakespeare family's insistence that she deliver indoors, Agnes gives birth to twins: Hamnet and Judith. Judith appears stillborn, but Agnes insists on holding her despite superstition, and the baby revives.

Seeing William's frustration with his writing, Agnes and her brother Bartholomew arrange to send him to London to pursue a theatrical career. He goes. He succeeds. He returns intermittently. The twins grow up close, frequently swapping clothes to trick their family.

Eleven years pass. William is now successful in London. In Stratford, Judith contracts the bubonic plague. Hamnet, devoted to his twin sister, lies beside her and invokes the story of their mother's hawk, whose spirit Agnes told them would carry their wishes. Hamnet tells death he wants to trade places with his sister.

Judith recovers. Hamnet falls gravely ill and dies. On his deathbed, he envisions himself on a stage, calling for his mother. Agnes's hawk appears.

William rushes home to find his son lying in repose. His grief strains the marriage. He buys the largest house in Stratford but cannot stay. He returns to London and begins writing Hamlet, struggling with his cast's inability to deliver the emotional truth he needs. In despair, he leans over the Thames and recites the "To be, or not to be" soliloquy.

Four years later, Agnes discovers that a play called Hamlet is being performed at the Globe Theatre. Initially furious that her son's name has been used (the film's prologue establishes that Hamnet and Hamlet were considered the same name in Elizabethan England), she travels to London with Bartholomew to confront William.

Finding him absent from home, Agnes goes to the Globe to see the performance. What follows is the film's climax: Agnes watches Hamlet and realizes, gradually, that the play is not a profanation of her son's name but a tribute to him. William appears on stage as the Ghost of Hamlet's father. The scenes between the Ghost and the Prince become a father speaking to his dead son. Agnes is moved to tears.

Backstage, William weeps. During Hamlet's death scene, Agnes reaches forward toward the dying actor, echoing the gesture she made when she first touched William's hand. The rest of the audience reaches with her. She envisions Hamnet on the stage, smiling, walking through a door that resembles the forest cave from the film's opening.

For the first time since her son's death, Agnes laughs and smiles. The film ends.

4. Woke Trap Assessment

This is NOT a woke trap.

Hamnet's feminist perspective is the openly stated thesis of both the source novel and the film. Maggie O'Farrell has been explicit in interviews that her novel was a deliberate reclamation of Shakespeare's wife from the margins of history. Chloe Zhao has spoken publicly about her desire to revive 'feminine consciousness' in her filmmaking. The marketing foregrounds Jessie Buckley, not Paul Mescal. No one walking into this film is being deceived about what they are getting.

Moreover, unlike films such as Conclave, which use traditional packaging to deliver progressive ideological payloads, Hamnet's feminist elements are inseparable from its genuinely traditional virtues. The film's feminist argument is that Agnes was a great mother, a devoted wife, and the emotional foundation of a household that produced genius. That is not a progressive dismantling of traditional values. It is a re-centering of who gets credit within a traditional family structure.

The film does not argue that marriage is bad, that men are toxic, or that Western civilization needs tearing down. It argues that the woman behind the genius deserves to be seen. You can disagree with the specific historical liberties, but the underlying values are more traditional than they first appear.

5. The Culture War Question: Is Hamnet Woke?

This is the question our readers will be asking, and the answer is nuanced.

What the film does that progressive critics celebrate:

  • Centers Agnes over Shakespeare, elevating the 'invisible wife' to protagonist status
  • Portrays Agnes as a wild, intuitive healer connected to nature, drawing on the 'reclaimed witch' archetype popular in contemporary feminist literature
  • Frames Shakespeare's genius as dependent on his wife's emotional sacrifice
  • The New Yorker noted the film 'means to deliver a feminist corrective to the myth of male genius'
  • Ms. Magazine listed it among the 'top feminist moments in pop culture' for 2025

What the film does that traditional viewers should appreciate:

  • Marriage is central and depicted as sacred even when strained by grief
  • Motherhood is the film's supreme value, portrayed as heroic and self-sacrificing
  • The death of a child is treated with devastating moral seriousness
  • There is zero identity politics, zero race-swapping, zero anachronistic modern lecturing
  • The cast is historically faithful to the period
  • Art (Hamlet) is depicted as a transcendent human achievement, not deconstructed or debunked
  • Shakespeare is not a villain. He is a flawed, grieving man who channels his loss into the greatest play ever written
  • The film's climax celebrates the power of great literature to heal, connect, and give meaning to suffering

The honest assessment: Hamnet is a feminist film that conservative audiences can watch without feeling ambushed. It is the rare prestige film that wears its perspective openly while also genuinely honoring traditional values of family, faith, sacrifice, and artistic greatness. The NYT op-ed made a perceptive point: the film's 'cultural politics align with feminist attempts to elevate Anne's influence on his work, as well as with conservative worldviews that prefer to imagine him as a heterosexual married man.' Hamnet sits at a genuine intersection.

6. Creative Team At A Glance

Director: Chloe Zhao (Chinese-American, b. 1982) - Oscar winner for Nomadland (2020). Self-described 'coastal liberal' with deep feminist sensibilities. Her work consistently centers marginalized perspectives, but she is a genuine artist, not an activist. She faced backlash in China for comments about its political system and operates as an outsider in multiple cultures.

Screenwriters: Chloe Zhao and Maggie O'Farrell. O'Farrell co-wrote the screenplay from her own award-winning novel. She was deliberate in wanting a director who was not 'steeped in Shakespeare' to avoid centering the male genius. The collaboration is genuine and respectful of the source material.

Producers: Liza Marshall (Hera Pictures), Pippa Harris, Nicolas Gonda, Steven Spielberg (Amblin Entertainment), Sam Mendes (Neal Street Productions). The Spielberg involvement signals the film's positioning as mainstream prestige, not activist cinema.

Cast: Jessie Buckley, Paul Mescal, Emily Watson, Joe Alwyn, Noah Jupe, Jacobi Jupe. All white, all British or Irish, all historically appropriate. Nina Gold's casting work earned an Oscar nomination.

7. Director/Writer Ideological Track Record

Chloe Zhao is a progressive filmmaker, but she is not an ideologue. Her body of work tells stories of people on the margins: Lakota Sioux horsemen, van-dwelling nomads, Shakespeare's forgotten wife. She approaches these subjects with genuine empathy and artistic ambition rather than political agendas. Nomadland won Best Picture without anyone calling it 'woke,' because it was too humane and too well-made to be reduced to ideology.

Her biggest misstep was Eternals (2021), which included Marvel's first openly gay superhero and drew conservative criticism for feeling more like a checkbox exercise than organic storytelling. Hamnet represents a return to the territory where Zhao works best: intimate, emotionally raw stories about people history has overlooked.

Zhao has spoken about wanting to revive 'feminine consciousness' in her films, which is an explicitly feminist framing. But her execution in Hamnet does not demonize masculinity or dismantle tradition. She gives Shakespeare genuine dignity, real talent, and authentic grief. She simply argues that Agnes deserves equal screen time in the story of her own family.

Maggie O'Farrell is a literary novelist, not a political activist. Her novel Hamnet was a work of speculative historical fiction that imagined the emotional interior of a family about which almost nothing is known. The feminist perspective is organic to the project: if you tell the story of Shakespeare's household from his wife's perspective, the result will inevitably be a feminist work. O'Farrell has not engaged in culture war discourse and has no significant public political activism beyond the inherent politics of telling a woman's story.

8. Adult Viewer Insight - What the Film Is Actually Arguing

Sophisticated adult viewers should understand the film's argument clearly.

The film's thesis, stated plainly:

1. Agnes was the emotional foundation of the Shakespeare household. She raised the children, healed the sick, managed the home while William was in London. His art was possible because of her sacrifice. This is feminist revisionism, but it is also probably true in broad strokes for most marriages in most historical periods.

2. Shakespeare's genius was fueled by personal loss. The film argues that Hamlet was born from the death of Hamnet, and that the play's emotional power comes from a father processing the most devastating thing a human can experience. This is speculative but widely discussed among Shakespeare scholars.

3. Art has the power to heal grief. The climactic Globe Theatre scene argues that Hamlet gave both Agnes and William a way to process their son's death. This is not a progressive or conservative argument. It is an argument about the purpose of art that would have been recognized by Aristotle.

4. The 'earth mother' archetype is valid and powerful. Agnes's connection to nature, herbs, hawks, and folk healing is romanticized as a form of feminine wisdom. This draws on the 'reclaimed witch' tradition popular in feminist circles. Some conservative viewers will find this hokey or vaguely pagan. Others will recognize it as a pre-modern folk Christianity that was common in Elizabethan England.

What the film does well: It is genuinely moving. Buckley's performance is extraordinary. The cinematography by Lukasz Zal (who shot Cold War and Ida) is austere and gorgeous. Max Richter's score is devastating. The Globe Theatre sequence is one of the great climactic scenes in recent cinema. The film earns every tear it wrings out of you.

What it does not do: It does not attack men, Western civilization, Christianity, or Shakespeare himself. It does not insert modern political discourse into a period setting. It does not race-swap or gender-swap. It does not sneer at tradition. It tells a story about a mother who lost her child, and a father who turned that loss into art.

Conservative viewers who avoid this film out of suspicion that it is a feminist takedown of Shakespeare will be missing one of the most genuinely humane and emotionally powerful films of 2025.

9. Parental Guidance

Rated PG-13 for thematic content, some strong sexuality, and partial nudity.

  • Themes: The death of a child from the bubonic plague is the film's central event. Shown with devastating emotional realism. Grief, marital strain, and loss permeate the second half. These themes are intense but handled with maturity and seriousness, not gratuitously.
  • Sexual content: One sex scene between Agnes and William (their initial consummation) with partial nudity. Several childbirth scenes with some partial nudity. A few kissing scenes. Nothing explicit or gratuitous.
  • Violence: Minimal. No graphic violence. Sword-fighting scenes are depicted within the Globe Theatre performance of Hamlet. The plague is shown through illness and death, not through gore.
  • Language: Period-appropriate. No modern profanity.
  • Spiritual content: Agnes's herbalism, palm-reading, and connection to nature could be interpreted as pagan or folk-mystical. The film treats it as pre-modern folk tradition rather than as explicit paganism. An Anglo-Saxon herbal charm (the Nine Herbs Charm) is quoted. Christian elements are present but not foregrounded.

Age recommendation: Mature teenagers (15+) who can handle the emotional intensity of a child's death. Younger children should not see this film. The plague death scene is harrowing in its realism. Parents should watch first and gauge their child's emotional readiness.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Chloe Zhao

Progressive feminist with deep interest in marginalized perspectives. Self-described 'coastal liberal' who has spoken extensively about recovering 'feminine consciousness' in her filmmaking. Her work consistently centers outsiders: nomads in Nomadland, an overlooked wife in Hamnet.

Beijing-born Chinese-American filmmaker (b. 1982). Won Best Director and Best Picture at the 93rd Academy Awards for Nomadland (2020), becoming the first woman of color and the second woman ever to win Best Director. Her early films, Songs My Brothers Taught Me (2015) and The Rider (2017), used non-professional actors to tell stories of marginalized communities on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. Her pivot to Marvel's Eternals (2021) was commercially successful but received mixed reviews. Zhao has described her filmmaking philosophy as driven by a desire to explore 'the tension between impossible polarities' and to revive 'feminine consciousness that has been destroyed in our civilization for tens of thousands of years.' Hamnet marks her return to prestige filmmaking and represents her most accomplished work since Nomadland.

Writer: Chloe Zhao & Maggie O'Farrell

O'Farrell is a British-Irish novelist born in Northern Ireland (b. 1972). Her novel Hamnet (2020) won the Women's Prize for Fiction and the National Book Critics Circle Award. The novel was O'Farrell's deliberate feminist reclamation of Shakespeare's wife, whom she renamed Agnes (the name listed in her father's will) to distinguish her from the actress Anne Hathaway. O'Farrell has been open about her intent to tell the story of Shakespeare's domestic life from the perspective of the woman history forgot. Zhao co-wrote the screenplay, and the two collaborated closely, with O'Farrell noting she wanted a director who 'wasn't particularly steeped in Shakespeare' so the film wouldn't put him center stage. The screenplay faithfully adapts the novel's feminist lens while amplifying the visual and elemental symbolism.

Adult Viewer Insight

Hamnet is a feminist film that conservative audiences can watch without feeling ambushed. Its perspective is openly stated, not hidden. Chloe Zhao centers Agnes over Shakespeare and argues that the wife's emotional labor made the husband's genius possible. This is feminist revisionism. But the film's underlying values are startlingly traditional: marriage is sacred, motherhood is heroic, the death of a child is the worst thing that can happen to a family, and great art is born from real suffering, not from ideology. There is zero identity politics, zero race-swapping, zero anachronistic social commentary. The cast is historically faithful. Shakespeare is not a villain. The Globe Theatre climax celebrates Hamlet as one of humanity's supreme artistic achievements. The honest truth is that Hamnet is the rarest kind of prestige film: one where the feminist perspective and the traditional values are genuinely compatible. Conservative viewers who skip it out of reflexive suspicion will miss one of the best films of 2025.

Parental Guidance

Rated PG-13 for thematic content, some strong sexuality, and partial nudity. The central event is the death of an 11-year-old boy from the bubonic plague, depicted with intense emotional realism. One sex scene with partial nudity. Several childbirth scenes. No graphic violence or modern profanity. The film's emotional intensity is the primary concern for younger viewers. The plague death sequence is harrowing and will be difficult for sensitive viewers of any age. Agnes's herbalism and folk healing could raise questions about paganism vs. Christianity for families who want to discuss it. Recommended for mature teenagers (15+) who can handle serious grief themes. Parents should watch first.
